title: Should the Church Stay Out of Politics?
excerpt: The church has been told to stay out of politics since a royal priest said it to Amos. It has failed in two opposite ways, by lending the cross to rulers and by keeping silent while neighbors were wronged, and four Christian traditions still disagree about where it should stand.
body:
Three people have each stopped going to a church, and politics is the reason every time. The first left because the sermons had turned into campaign speeches, and he could no longer tell where the Bible stopped and the candidate began. The second left a different congregation in a year when her neighbors were being wronged in plain sight. Her pastor said nothing about it for twelve months and described his silence as keeping to spiritual things. The third is a pastor. In one week he received two letters, one telling him he had become too political and one calling him a coward.

A skeptic has a simpler view of all three. When the church had power, he says, it used that power to coerce, and now that it has lost it, it asks for tolerance. The decent arrangement is for religion to stay private, a thing people do at home and on Sunday, and for public life to go on without it.

He has much of the history right. But to say that the church should stay out of politics can mean at least four things, and they don't stand or fall together. It can mean that the church should never use the state's power to enforce its faith. It can mean that pulpits should not endorse rulers or factions. It can mean that Christians should not vote or hold office. Or it can mean that the church should say nothing about public wrongs. Christians have answered each of those differently, and the history shows what the answers cost.

## What the Bible Shows

Jesus refused political power every time it was offered. After he fed a crowd, they meant "to come and take him by force to make him king," and he "withdrew again to the mountain by himself" (John 6:15). In the wilderness the devil offered him the kingdoms of the world, and he turned them down (Luke 4:5–8). On trial for his life he told the Roman governor, "My kingdom is not of this world" (John 18:36).

He also would not treat the ruler as beyond comment. Asked whether it was lawful to pay Caesar's tax, he had them produce the coin and say whose image was on it. "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's" (Mark 12:17). The sentence grants Caesar something, and by granting it sets a limit. Whatever belongs to God is not Caesar's to claim.

Around him stand prophets who spoke to kings directly. John the Baptist told the local ruler about his marriage, "It is not lawful for you" (Mark 6:18), and was beheaded for it. Elijah met King Ahab in a vineyard whose owner the crown had arranged to kill, and asked him, "Have you killed and also taken possession?" (1 Kings 21:19). When Amos preached judgment at the royal shrine, the priest in charge told him to go home and never to "prophesy at Bethel, for it is the king's sanctuary, and it is a temple of the kingdom" (Amos 7:13). It is an early instruction to a preacher to keep out of the king's business, and it came from the priest of the king's own sanctuary.

The apostles hold two things together. Paul calls the governing authority "God's servant for your good" (Romans 13:4) and tells the church to pray "for kings and all who are in high positions" (1 Timothy 2:2). The book of Revelation shows the same empire as a beast that demands worship (Revelation 13:7–8). And when the authorities in Jerusalem ordered the apostles to stop preaching, the reply was short: "We must obey God rather than men" (Acts 5:29).

So the New Testament gives the church no program for governing, and it gives no permission for silence either. It gives a Lord whom rulers answer to, and a people who honor the ruler and are prepared to refuse him.

## 312 and After

For three centuries the church had no power to misuse. Then, in October of 312, Constantine won the western empire, and within a year Christianity was legal. By 380 it was the empire's official faith. The gain was real. The persecutions were over, and nobody who had lived through them thought that a small thing.

The cost came quickly. In the 380s a Spanish ascetic named Priscillian was accused of heresy, and the imperial authorities, urged on by bishops, put him to death. The church that had been killed by the state had learned to use the state to kill.

A few years later came the opposite scene. After the emperor Theodosius ordered a massacre in Thessalonica, Ambrose, the bishop of Milan, told him that he could not come to the Lord's table until he had done public penance. The emperor did it. Ambrose commanded no soldiers. He spoke as a pastor to a member of his church who had blood on his hands.

Those two scenes, a few years apart, mark out the whole problem. The history course on this site says of that century, "Every generation since has faced its own version of 312, some throne or party or public offering the church protection in exchange for blessing, and the offer never stops sounding like providence." Another essay here tells [how the church came to marry the empire](/writing/when-the-church-married-empire).

Augustine, writing as that empire began to fall, gave the church its most lasting way of thinking about this. There are two cities, he said, formed by two loves, and they are mixed together until the end. The heavenly city "calls citizens out of all nations" and makes use of the earthly city's peace while it travels. On his account no empire is the kingdom of God, Rome included, and no Christian is excused from caring about the peace of the city he lives in.

## Four Ways of Standing

The Reformation broke the medieval arrangement, in which popes and kings had fought for centuries over who stood above whom, and it left four accounts that are still with us.

The Lutheran account speaks of two kingdoms. God rules the world in two ways, through the gospel in the church and through law and the sword in the state, and the two are not to be mixed. The Lutheran confession of 1530 says that "the power of the Church and the civil power must not be confounded," and of the church, "Let it not break into the office of another." A Christian may be a judge or a soldier or a prince, and serves God there. The strength of this account is that it protects the gospel from being turned into legislation and protects the citizen from a clergy with police powers. The question it has been asked ever since the 1930s is whether a church trained to leave the state to its own business has anything to say when the state does evil.

The Reformed account gives the ruler a higher calling and the church a wider claim. John Calvin called civil office "a calling not only holy and legitimate, but far the most sacred and honourable in human life," and held that government exists in part "to cherish and support the external worship of God." The Westminster Confession of 1646 made it the magistrate's duty to see "that all blasphemies and heresies be suppressed." Most Reformed churches long ago gave up that last claim. What they kept is the conviction, as this site's study of church and state puts it, that there is "no sphere sealed off from Christ," and that conviction has built schools, hospitals and movements of reform. The question for this account is Geneva in 1553, when Michael Servetus was burned for denying the Trinity with Calvin's approval. If Christ's claim covers public life, it has to be settled who enforces the claim, and by what means.

The Anabaptist account refuses the whole arrangement. Meeting at Schleitheim in 1527, its first leaders agreed that "it is not appropriate for a Christian to serve as a magistrate," because "their citizenship is in this world, but the Christian's citizenship is in heaven." They pointed to the day the crowd wanted to crown Jesus: "They wished to make Christ king, but He fled." On this account the church serves the world by being a different kind of society, with its own way of handling money, enemies and power. Its strength is that it saw early what the state churches were doing with the sword, and its members were hunted for a century by Catholics and Protestants alike. The question for it is whether a people who will not govern may still benefit from those who do, and whether separation can become a reason to say nothing while a neighbor is being wronged.

The fourth is the older Catholic account that descends from Augustine. The state is good within its limits, the common good is every Christian's concern, and the kingdom of God is never to be confused with any government. Its question is its own medieval record, when the church did not merely advise kings but claimed to stand above them.

How church and state should relate is a question of the second order. Faithful churches hold each of these four, and this essay does not choose among them. A companion essay looks at [what it would mean for a nation to be Christian](/writing/can-a-nation-be-christian).

## Two Churches That Could Not Stay Out

Twice in the modern period the question stopped being theoretical.

The first was in America. For Black Christians politics was never something a person could decline to be involved in, because the law itself said who owned them. In 1794 Richard Allen and Absalom Jones, two leaders of the Black church in Philadelphia, printed an address to slaveholders. "If you love your children, if you love your country, if you love the God of love," they wrote, "clear your hands from slaves, burden not your children or country with them." That was a sermon and a political act in the same sentence. A good many white churches, in the decades that followed, held that slavery was a civil matter on which the pulpit should keep quiet. The Black church went on speaking for a hundred and seventy years. In 1963 Martin Luther King Jr., a Baptist preacher, wrote his letter from a Birmingham jail to white clergymen who had urged him to wait.

The second was in Germany. When Hitler came to power in 1933, most German Protestants welcomed him. A movement calling itself the German Christians set out to merge church and regime, and adopted the state's racial rules, so that a pastor of Jewish descent could be barred from a pulpit. In May of 1934 a minority met at Barmen and answered with a declaration. Its first thesis confessed that Jesus Christ "is the one Word of God which we have to hear and which we have to trust and obey in life and in death." Its second rejected the idea that there are "areas of our life in which we would not belong to Jesus Christ, but to other lords." Its fifth rejected the claim that the state could become "the single and totalitarian order of human life."

Barmen was brave, and the history course on this site is plain about its limit. It "said nothing directly about the persecution of the Jews, and most of its signers never did either." It defended the church. In 1945 the surviving leaders confessed in public that they had not been courageous enough.

The two cases show the two opposite failures. The German Christians put the church at the service of a nation and its ruler. The white churches that kept quiet about slavery, and most of the German church after 1934, did the other thing. They kept the faith indoors while their neighbors were destroyed, and called it staying out of politics.

## Two Errors and One Root

The first error has a current name. The page on this site that examines [whether Christian nationalism is Christian](/questions/morality/is-christian-nationalism-christian) defines it as "the claim that a nation should be Christian as a nation, in its laws, its customs and its rulers' duties." The people who hold it are not fools, and some of what they say is right. Love of country is no sin, and no law is morally neutral. But that page reaches a conclusion, and this essay keeps it: "This site doesn't teach Christian nationalism as true. It says so with grief, and it applies the same test to any cause, on any side, that drafts the cross."

That last clause matters. A congregation can be captured from either direction. One church comes to hear the nation's strength and its inherited way of life as the gospel's own cause, and it reads its Bible for whatever supports them. Another comes to hear a program for remaking society as the kingdom of God arriving, and it reads its Bible for whatever supports that. Each can describe the other's captivity exactly. Another essay here measures both by [the same standard](/writing/why-jesus-wont-fit-in-either-party).

The second error is the one the skeptic recommends, a faith with nothing to say in public. It sounds humble. But Barmen's second thesis was written against it, and so was the book of Amos. A church that will speak about the sins of private life and never about cruelty done by law has not avoided politics. It has taken the side of whatever is already happening.

The two errors look like opposites, and they grow from one root. Both let something other than Christ decide when the church speaks. In the first case the ruler or the movement decides. In the second it is the congregation's comfort.

We have committed both, and often the same congregation has done so in different decades. We have asked the government to do for the church what the church had stopped doing for itself. We have gone quiet exactly when speaking would cost us members or money. And we are quick to see the politics in the church across town and slow to see it in our own.

The history offers a few distinctions that most of the four accounts could accept. A church that names a wrong is doing something different from a church that names a candidate. Persuading neighbors is different from compelling them. And what a Christian does as a citizen, with a vote or an office, is different from what the church says as the church, with its Lord's name attached. Ambrose stayed on the first side of each of those lines. The bishops who went to the emperor about Priscillian did not.

## What Is Settled and What Is Not

Christians confess that Jesus Christ is Lord of every ruler and every nation, that governments are to be honored and prayed for, that no state may be given what belongs to God, and that when the two commands collide the church obeys God. They confess that the church is gathered from all nations and is no nation's possession.

How the church should relate to the state, and whether Christians serve best by governing or by standing apart, are questions on which faithful churches differ. What party or policy a Christian should support is not something this essay addresses, and it names none.

On the morning of his death Jesus stood in a governor's court, which is as political a room as there is. He didn't call for the governor's overthrow, and he didn't ask for the governor's chair. He also didn't keep quiet. He did not deny that he was a king, and he said he had come to bear witness to the truth, and the governor, who had an empire behind him, asked, "What is truth?" (John 18:38) and went out without waiting for a reply. The church has been in that room ever since. It has wanted the chair, and it has wanted to slip out the door, and it has rarely been content to stand where he stood and say what he said.

*"Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's."* (Mark 12:17)

*"We must obey God rather than men."* (Acts 5:29)
